utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, can you following the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and also good afternoon to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, I am here together with co-counsel Ms. Patricia Sellers, and Ms. Joanne Richardson, as well as our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Vasvija Vidovic and Mr. John Jones, appearing on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us today is our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, as well as our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team. So I understand there are some preliminaries. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to update you further and the Defence team, we would like to provide you with a new updated witness list for the weeks to come. May I ask the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This chain of custody evidence, what is it about? Which chain of custody are you referring to? Witnesses 40 -- witnesses 50, 51, 50, 52 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And 53, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 50. These are all documents already put into evidence in which the Defence team has questions and argued that chain of custody didn't show information to the full extent with a view to the chain. When it comes to 52, 53, it is the Sokolac collection, and 50 it is the Banja Luka collection documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was -- I was thinking -- obviously I don't know how much information is entailed, although I see three hours, three hours, three hours, three hours. But why don't we do it in a different way? Why don't you prepare written statements -- these persons are available here or -- in The Hague or are they --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: They are available for -- well, this is of course our tentative list. We have to schedule for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what I was going to suggest, Madam Vidovic and Mr. Jones, that these three, four witnesses -- three or four, I don't know whether they are three or four --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yeah, three, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Three, will make a written statement which will be filed and presented under the Rule 92 bis. And then if they are made available in good time, you will just indicate whether you want to cross-examine these either -- any or all of these three witnesses. I reckon instead of having three days, we can do this probably in one day, if it is agreeable to you. I mean as far as Rule 92 bis statement examination-in-chief in the form of a statement is concerned, it's up to you. I mean, I can't enforce it of course. I can enforce it if I want to, but I don't mean to enforce it unless you really want to do it. And provided it is acceptable also to -- to the Defence, who can then limit their cross-examination to the basis -- if at all necessary, because you might come to the conclusion that there is enough information that you don't need to cross-examine any or all of these witnesses. That's up to you. Think about it, Mr. Wubben. I mean, I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We'll think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I have caught both of you maybe on the wrong foot, so I don't surprise anyone or expect an answer today. We'll talk about it tomorrow. But I think it can be done, I mean, without any problems at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. We will continue with this witness now. May I refer you to witness number 44 on this list that you have just filed and remind you that if you are seeking the -- to keep in place the protective measures that were granted to this witness in the beginning, you need to file a written motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In that respect, we will do so. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But please do notice that if this witness is due to start supposedly on the 2nd of May, you need to do that fairly quickly. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher -- I'm sorry, are there any preliminary issues that you would like to raise, Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are none, Your Honours. But we would like to ask the OTP to do whatever is within their power to give us as soon as possible the testimonies of these witnesses, especially Witness Number 51, and to provide these in the Bosnian language as soon as possible, namely we need to consult our client on these matters beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm saying maybe you can deal with 50, 52, and 53 in a -- in the format that I suggested because 51, I would imagine, is a very important witness, and you will probably need much more than the five hours that you are indicating here. Anyway, it's up to you. Tell us -- come back to us tomorrow. Let's see what happened to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, for cross-examination, Madam Vidovic, how much time do you require? Today for sure and tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it depends on how many documents or new matters will be raised by the Prosecution. My idea was for this cross-examination to be brought to an end within three and a half or four hours. However, if the OTP introduces new documents, raising new issues, that probably means I'll take longer than I expected to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Good afternoon to you. Welcome back. Again, two things: Please do -- I am reminding you that you are testifying under oath. Secondly, if there are problems with interpretation, let me know straight away. You may sit down, and we will start immediately so as not to lose more time. Yes, Ms. Richardson, how long do you think you will need to finish your in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I assured the Court that I will move expediently and I will try to wrap up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Expeditiously as well, Your Honour. And I will try to wrap up before the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that means the witness will be here tomorrow. Okay. Let's -- I'll stop you if I think you're covering areas which we've covered already or which don't need as much coverage as you've been giving some. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Becirovic. Last Thursday you were testifying about the use of the radio IC-745 which communications or messages were sent -- which radio was located in the PTT building. I'd like to draw your attention to this specific matter and ask you whether or not members of the Territorial Defence used this radio while you were at the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio that was used there was 751. I think you said 745 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that members of the Territorial Defence, in cases where they tried to stay in touch with their families using this equipment, their families that were this Tuzla further afield, had the chance of using the equipment under my control, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Which members of the territorial staff used the equipment? Please give us their names.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No exception. All of them had an opportunity to make use of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you give us the names of the individuals that you recalled who used the equipment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, Mr. Naser Oric used my services to keep in contact with his family. His family was in Slovenia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when -- could you tell us about the circumstances surrounding the use of Mr. -- of the radio by Mr. Naser Oric to contact his family. First tell us when did he come to the PTT building, if that's where this in fact occurred?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all the dates. It occurred every once in a while, perhaps once a month or even less. That's how often he came to get in touch with his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall what month and what year?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the first time was in the month of August, but I can't be sure. It may have been September 1992 as well. As time went by and depending on the situation that prevailed in Srebrenica municipality, he came less and less often. I suppose the reason was that his presence was far more required elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let's talk about when the first time -- when was the first time that he came to the PTT building. Could you tell us about the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he wanted to call his family. I don't think he knew at the time how the radio device was supposed to be operated or how communication could be established using the radio. I had the feeling that I could be of service to him the very moment he came, and I think he was surprised when I explained to him that this was in fact not the case, when I explained how this equipment functioned, that I should first locate a ham radio operator based in Slovenia who was willing to make a phone call to his wife to make contact, or maybe tell his wife to come and see him at his flat, this ham radio operator's flat, depending on where he worked from, where he was based. Then a time was to be set. This ham radio operator was supposed to inform my -- me as the communications officer on our side, and then I would tell Naser Oric when communication could be established. Naser Oric was perhaps puzzled at the time to hear this explanation, but he accepted it as a fact. It was soon after, perhaps two or three days after, I really can't remember, it took me a couple of days to arrange this and get in touch with the ham radio operator in Crnomelj called Miralem. Miralem said that he was willing to do this. He made a phone call to Mr. Naser Oric's wife. He agreed with her for her to go from Ljubljana to Crnomelj. He informed me about this and then I in turn informed Naser Oric that two or three days later was the time, and we should set a specific time for him to talk to his wife, and that was what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how often did he come to the PTT building to establish communication with his wife in Ljubljana?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time. My impression is once a month or less, but I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Oric use the radio to contact anyone else?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I think February of 1993, he once used the radio to get in touch with a person called Munja who was in Tuzla. And once he used it to get in touch with President Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let's take this one at a time. Regarding his communication with Munja in Tuzla, could you tell the Trial Chamber about those set of circumstances when he contacted this individual? And please also tell us the year. I believe you've already said February of 1993, excuse me, so just tell us about the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened at a time when the Serbs were carrying out a heavy offensive against Cerska, Kamenica, and Konjevic Polje. Naser Oric called Munja from Konjevic Polje following a request by Munja through his club 4-BMN. Nada sat next to the radio equipment in Tuzla. They talked once or twice, I'm not sure. Munja wanted to know about the situation in Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica. If I remember correctly, and I believe I do remember the gist of their conversation, Naser requested that the armed forces from Tuzla and the broader Tuzla region get involved a bit more seriously in trying to lift the blockade of the free territory of Srebrenica; that was the crux of their conversation. Munja appeared to be hopeful that something could be done, but we now know that nothing in fact happened at the time except what Munja tried to explain, what he in fact said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who is Munja? Do you recall who he was? Any position that he held in Tuzla and any organisation he was affiliated with?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about his real name. I only know the person's nickname, Munja. I don't know what his affiliations were, but based on the promises he made back then that the army based in Tuzla would do something about the Srebrenica situation, my assumption was that he may have been a member of the armed forces in the Tuzla area. But I must say this again, I simply don't know whether he was or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you testified that he contacted or -- let me rephrase the question. Was he the one who initiated contact with Naser Oric and could you tell us how it was that he did that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Munja initiated contact -- this is how it happened. Nada from 4-BMN, it was a radio club in Tuzla, called me to tell me that there was a gentleman who requested to talk to Naser.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how did you learn his name was Munja?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nada told me. She was the one who told me. She said, Munja is the person. First she asked me, that's if I remember correctly, if I knew who the person was. And then as we continued -- when we got in touch, when we introduced himself, he said that his nickname was Munja.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the word actually means lightning, a bolt of lightning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who scheduled the time for the telephone -- excuse me, for the discussion between Munja and Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember all the details now. One thing I can say though is the moment someone asked me to get in contact with Naser or anyone else, I was not given to promising anything, or the other way around. It may have been the case the if Naser said that he was in a position to be near the radio device at a given time, that he was the one who actually set the time for their contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was Naser Oric known by any other name during this time that you -- that he used the radio?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think at the time the nickname he was using was Gazda, boss.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did Nada or anyone else refer to him by this name?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for Nada to talk to Naser. Whenever Nada and I established a line of communication, we'd just hand the mikes over to Munja on Nada's side or Naser on my side, and they would do the talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When was this name used, Gazda?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Naser Oric say to Munja?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained a while ago that Naser had asked Munja that the armed forces from Tuzla do something to help lift the blockade of the three territories of Cerska, Kamenica, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica in order to make life easier for the people who remained in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How many conversations did he have with Munja to your knowledge and was it all -- was this all in February of 1993 or some time the next month?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think two or three, possibly four but not more. All of their conversations occurred within a single month. Those were brief conversations, and I didn't realise at the time that they had led to anything. It was necessary to try to do something to help the people who had been subjected to heavy attacks in the area of Konjevic Polje, Cerska, and Srebrenica, and that's what I believe the conversations were actually about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You testified that he -- that Naser Oric also contacted Izetbegovic. Could you tell the Trial Chamber about the circumstances of that communication and when that in fact occurred?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't give you a date, I think it was in early March 2003 [as interpreted]. There was an enemy offensive against Srebrenica, a furious one at the time. Many women, civilians, and soldiers or killed. There was a great number of casualties and a general state of confusion where it was impossible to tell whether you would make it to the next day, whether anyone would. So those were the circumstances when Naser talked to President Izetbegovic. In this conversation, he told the president about the situation in Srebrenica and asked for help. I'm not sure if he actually defined the kind of help that he was seeking, but I think he said any sort of help just to stop the attacks and to stop the killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did there come a time -- how many conversations did he have with Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was just one conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did there come a time, Mr. Becirovic, that you arranged for another conversation -- another contact wherein Mr. Oric had a conversation with someone in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser Oric never talked to anyone else in Sarajevo, with the exception of President Izetbegovic. Had it been necessary, it would have been possible to arrange.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Other than in -- in 1993, other than President Izetbegovic, who else did he speak with, other than Izetbegovic and Munja; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, Your Honours. There was another contact that Naser Oric made. He got in touch with Sefer Halilovic. It escaped me a while ago when I said he hadn't talked to anyone else. I think this was also in March, early March, I think, 1993. The gist of the conversation was the same as the one with President Izetbegovic. There was a difficult situation and one had to find a way to overcome this situation and to help people in the Srebrenica area, in part of the Srebrenica area. People needed help in order to survive, because February and March are known as months when people starved in the area. The situation was worsening severely concerning hygiene, and there were continual onslaughts by the Serb forces. There were artillery attacks and infantry attacks, and infection spread throughout the area as well. It was a situation that could no longer be allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber about the -- could you tell the Trial Chamber what was discussed between Naser Oric and Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, the gist of the conversation was the same as the one that he had with President Izetbegovic. It was an appeal for help, it was an appeal to stop the killing and to put an end to this state of chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "an appeal for help," was there any specific request made by Naser Oric or any specific response?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said any sort of help, any form of help, which would not have precluded the possibility for the armed forces in the area of Tuzla to set out and try to help lift the blockade of Srebrenica. This was seen at the time as the best way, but perhaps there were other ways that people had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was it a request for food, do you recall? Did that request include food? Or was it only military assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry -- he said it was an appeal for any help, so I don't see how it could be a request which was only for military assistance. The request is already as broad-ranging as it can possibly be. I don't object to the first part of the question whether food as requested, but it wouldn't be correct to characterise what has been said so far as a request only for military assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, believe I phrased the question as an "or." Food or military assistance. And I believe based on what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but you're limited. In other words, you are just -- while the witness said "any form of help," and he repeated it twice, and any kind of help that would try to help lift the blockade of Srebrenica, you're just limiting it to food or military assistance, which is not right. I mean, just --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What kind of help was discussed or requested or promised, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Naser Oric briefly described the situation that prevailed in the three municipalities of Bratunac, Zvornik, Vlasenica, and Srebrenica. In view of the fact that there was a great number of casualties, wounded and killed, the humanitarian situation was severe. There were no medications in the area. He sought any kind of help that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could be provided. He wasn't asking for anything in particular. At the time, the president of the War Presidency hailed in Avdic often sent out appeals for assistance in writing and in direct communication, oral communication, with President Izetbegovic. The requests that were written were sent to the highest international authorities as well, such as the Security Council. Our intention was to send out information on how critical our situation was. In addition to the civilian bodies of government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, these appeals were also sent to the high commission for -- commissioner for refugees. The numbers of refugees increased in the area. Those who had arrived in 1992 were joined by a new wave of refugees from the occupied territories of Kamenica, Cerska, and Konjevic Polje later on. In the second half of March, Srebrenica was a town holding as many as 25.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Becirovic, let me stop you. With respect to the areas you were going into, I would like you to focus in on the communication aspect now. Could you tell us where Naser Oric was when this conversation took place with Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation took place in Konjevic Polje. Mr. Naser Oric was in Konjevic Polje. There was a heavy Serbian attack underway on Konjevic Polje; Naser Oric was there. I was there, too, and that was where contact was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the means -- what communication equipment was used during this conversation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A short wave radio, Atlas 210X. It had been sent over to Cerska sometime previously in order to send information from Cerska to Srebrenica, and this information could not be sent out to the public and the bodies of government. There was a need for a piece of equipment to be sent to that area because there was none in the area. It was used to send information to the civilian bodies of government from the Cerska area and primarily to the general public, the media, the television. This is what the equipment was used for. There was an operator in Cerska who was in charge of the equipment, but he was not sufficiently skilled to be able to use it properly. There was an offensive underway, and I travelled to Cerska in order to teach the operator how to use the equipment, to teach him the skills that he lacked. In the meantime, Cerska had been occupied and this piece of equipment had been transferred to Konjevic Polje. So it was from Konjevic Polje that contact was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you can briefly recall if any other members of the Territorial Defence contacted -- used the PTT building and the IC-751 to make any contacts during the period of time that you were in Srebrenica, if you could recall the names just briefly?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the outset, I said that anyone who wished to get in touch with their families meet in Tuzla, Croatia, Slovenia, or elsewhere would be granted access and given an opportunity to establish communication. I provided my services. This in no way meant that members of the TO had any sort of priority status or indeed that they were the only ones who were allowed to use this equipment. Having said that, members of the Territorial Defence also used my services and also used this piece of equipment that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Without going into the details of the conversation, could you tell us whether any international organisations were able to use the PTT building and the radio to communicate?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When General Morillon arrived in Srebrenica, he installed his own staff in Srebrenica. He explained to the people that he wanted to stay to help them. While General Morillon was in Srebrenica, he established several contacts. At that time, I was informed that these contacts were established in order to provide information to the French television, and this was done with the help of the ham radio operators from Zagreb. In addition to the French television, General Morillon also established contact with some journalists from various papers who were stationed either in Sarajevo or in Zagreb. In addition to General Morillon, an official of the international organisation of Medicins Sans Frontieres, also used the services of our radio. He talked to people in Split. As I believe that there was an office of the organisation down there in Split, I believe that he talked to them about his requirements for medical supplies in Srebrenica at the time. This equipment was also used by a photographer from Germany who arrived in February 1993 in Srebrenica. His name was Philip von Retenhousen [phoen]. He spoke to ham radio operators from Berlin in order to convey messages to Reuters. Some other newspapers also used the same service in order to find out what was going on in Srebrenica. I would like to repeat that the IC-751 radio equipment was used to establish a number of contacts with Tillman Zilh, who was the president for the association of threatened nations in Germany, and the gist of the information was the same, the situation in Srebrenica, the humanitarian situation, the -- and any other such information. After the demilitarisation, there were contacts with other subjects, primarily with the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you there. Thank you, Mr. Becirovic. As far as you know during the time you were in the PTT building, did any of the other operators or yourself use the radio to discuss matters of exchange, exchanges of prisoners, with any of the Serbian authorities or anyone else for that matter?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never used the radio to talk to anybody about exchanges. I don't know that any of the operators who worked with me did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'd like to bring your attention back to your earlier testimony when you described for the Trial Chamber the equipment that you recovered in the information centre, and I believe you also mentioned the MUP as well. Did you recover any communication equipment that necessitated the use of codes?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found a piece of equipment in the early information centre that was used before the war for coding and decoding of written information. However, that piece of equipment was not used after the war started.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you conduct any type of prewar procedure with respect to this piece of equipment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What procedure do you have in mind? But I would like to respond by saying that I offered to the regional information centre to an official who worked there whom I knew personally to use this equipment if they wanted to. I gave them that option. However, in Srebrenica I never received any answer to that. Nobody ever told me to use it or not to use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Who in Srebrenica knew you were in possession of this equipment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that any of the people who were in Srebrenica at the time even knew what the purpose of this equipment was, if we're talking about this piece of equipment for coding and decoding, for encryption. Because all the people who knew how to use it had left Srebrenica before the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Other than the people who knew how to use it, did you tell anyone when you first found the equipment that -- that it was there, that you found it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I found it, it was intact. I told Akif Ustic that this piece of equipment was there. I explained to him what its purpose was. I can't remember what he said to me. I took the opportunity to give him and give the regional centre for information in Tuzla an option to use this equipment. I suppose that it is possible that he might have agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you able to determine whether this piece of equipment was working, operational?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The equipment was operational. Why am I saying this? The room where it was found had never been broken into. And also, its condition was good. I had used it before the war and I was in a position to know whether it was operational or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to this piece of equipment, do you recall conducting any prewar procedures regarding its operation, its ability to be operated?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There was no need for me to do that. Let me just put it simply: I didn't check it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'd like to bring your attention again to some of the other type of equipment that was recovered. You mentioned an Atlas that was sent to Cerska. Could you tell us a little bit more about this Atlas and tell us how many of them you recovered.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the information centre, we found two Atlas 210X pieces of equipment. One of them was transferred to Cerska and the other was not used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "not used," was it operational and where was it taken, if any place?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was operational. It could be used, somebody could use it, but nobody ever did. It was found, as I've already told you, in the information centre, communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was that where it was kept during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Up to the second half of 1993 it was kept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how big this Atlas is?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, its front panel is rectangular, it's about 50 centimetres wide, maybe some 20 centimetres high, and it's about 35 to 40 centimetres deep or long.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Other than the Atlas, what other type of communication equipment did you recover? And I believe you've already -- we've already covered the IC-751, the 745. Anything else that you recall?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three other radio sets that had been used by the civilian protection before the war. They were very small pieces of equipment with very short range of barely a few kilometres. They were a bit outdated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where was this piece of equipment kept?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jusuf Halilovic took over those pieces of equipment. Before the war he was the Chief of Staff of the civilian protection, and he continued performing that duty throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Any other type of equipment you recall recovering? I'm not sure if you testified to this earlier, so you can correct me if I'm wrong. Do you recall recovering an Iskra?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he mentioned this last Thursday or Wednesday or whenever --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to determine if that's the case, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did mention it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you did in fact recover this piece of equipment, where was it kept?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which particular piece of equipment are you now referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The piece of equipment that Your Honour just mentioned, the Iskra.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an Iskra equipment in the information centre, and it stayed there. Throughout the war, it was never used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was this piece of equipment also operational?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. If it was operational before the 17th of April, 1992, there is no reason for it not to be operational after that. It used the 220 volt energy, and when there was no electricity as of June 1992 it could not be used for that reason. And if you're asking me whether theoretically speaking it was operational, yes, it was operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'd like to just take you to another series of questions regarding communication equipment and ask you if you are familiar with whether or not the Territorial Defence in the surrounding areas of Srebrenica used any type of communication equipment.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any piece of equipment used for communication around Srebrenica. I only know that there were no such pieces of equipment. So if there weren't any, that means that they couldn't be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prior to the war, did the Territorial Defence -- were they in possession, as far as you know, of communication equipment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was some equipment that had been used by the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And are you -- could you tell us what types of equipments they were in possession of prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were UKT, the ultra high-frequency types of equipment called RUP-12, RUP-2B, and RUP-2/2/K.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to have the witness look at some photographs and have him tell us whether or not he can identify what's in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, does the witness know where these radios or these high frequency types of equipment were kept in prewar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war they were kept in the storage of the Territorial Defence Staff in Srebrenica. And as soon as the war broke out, they were transferred to the old primary school in Potocari. On the 18th of April, when the shelling started, this equipment suffered a certain degree of damage because the old primary school was shelled and it -- as a result of that, it was partly destroyed and partly damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I'd like to start with Prosecution's Exhibit P499, which is in Sanction, and then have the witness shown two new exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, if you could take a look at the screen in front of you and tell the Trial Chamber whether you recognise this piece of equipment that's before you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photo is not very clear. If I can see well, this could be the front panel of one of the radio -- radios that I have mentioned, but it is very hard for me to conclude which one of them it would be, just looking at this photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I quite agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps I don't think whether technically it is possible, dealing with Sanction, can we make it appear lighter, much lighter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think have another suggestion If I could have the registrar's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have one in colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. If we could show the witness that. I think it's much clearer -- it's black and white. I stand corrected. If we can show the witness this photograph, it's much clearer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this is indeed dark, very dark, at least on the screen, on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again the photo is blurred. It's very hard for me to tell you exactly what type of equipment it depicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you look at the photograph, is it similar to what you described as the RUP-12, although I know you've indicated that it's a bit dark?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we know that the front panel of this equipment has three switch buttons to determine the frequency, that it does have a switch for the antenna and that there's also the area where you mount the antenna, the area where you mount the microphone. It is possible that this is RUP-12. However, if I can remember well, I have not seen this type of equipment in a long time, but I remember that it did have these switches. Then it is possible that this looks similar like that equipment, but I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's not lose more time on this. Please --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can hand the witness the other two photos we'll mark them later. And could you tell us whether you recognise the equipment shown on them. Put them on the ELMO, please. Let's start with that one. Do you think you can tell us what equipment that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the right lower corner it says 2/2K, so this is the type of equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And it's an RU, again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And for the record, this photo is being given -- is being marked as Prosecution Exhibit P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P533.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P533. Next one. Do you recognise this equipment? It seems at the bottom there is RT or something, 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] RT-20TC -- 4, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this equipment? Was it amongst the equipment that the TO had before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. This piece of equipment -- I can't remember -- I believe that this type of equipment, judging by the number, the markings on it, belonged -- or was used by the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So this document will be marked as Prosecution Exhibit P534. So you've got two answers in one, Ms. Richardson. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, you mentioned that Potocari had an RUP-12. Could you tell us whether -- when they obtained this RUP-12?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry -- first of all, Potocari is a village. I don't know particularly whether that means that Potocari had an RUP-12. But I don't recall the witness mentioning that Potocari had an RUP-12. Perhaps he could be directed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness said that after the war, as soon as the war started all the transmitters or radio equipment that the TO had before the war was transported to the Potocari school. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Oh, I see, okay so. It refers to the location of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: School in Potocari. So I take it that what Ms. Richardson is seeking now is to establish when this transportation --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the danger is suggesting that Potocari as some sort of entity possessed these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, you are right. But, okay, we all understand that it isn't. Yes, when were they moved from Srebrenica to Potocari, the TO equipment, transmit -- radio equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember it was one or two weeks before the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what, if anything, happened to the equipment that was taken to the school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's already told us that it suffered damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the equipment that suffered damage, do you recall if anything was done with the equipment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the demilitarisation, several such pieces of equipment which were not in the working order were used to put something together that could be used, that could be operational. And I believe that four or five or maybe even six such new pieces of equipment resulted from that activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but in the meantime you've left empty an entire year; in other words, two weeks before the 17th of April, 1992, to the demilitarisation, which happened roughly a year -- a year later. So during that year, April 1992 to April 1993, what happened to this equipment that had been taken to Potocari? Was damaged, you said, or part of it was damaged. Was it left there? Was it never used to your knowledge? Or was it used, and if it was by whom, and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, nobody used that equipment. That equipment was partly destroyed. It was amongst the rubble of the school. And due to the lack of personnel that could use it -- I believe that nobody even -- it never occurred to anybody to use it. I went to the school in Potocari, having my reservations about the information that had reached me. I was hoping that some of this equipment may be rendered usable. However, when I saw the equipment I realised that it wouldn't be possible. I just took one piece of equipment to the information centre. It was not operational. I could not make it operational. And I believe at the time that without the skills of skilled persons, it would be impossible to use the equipment or to take two or three pieces to make one operational piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The radio -- the equipment that you said was destroyed in Potocari, did there ever come a time that an RUP was -- was fixed or made operational?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know in the village of Pale there was an RUP-12 that was operational. For the most part, it was used to listen in to whatever was going on on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the whole gist is: Was this radio or transmitter or receiver, RUP-12, in Pale constructed out of the bits and pieces of the other radios that had been destroyed in the Potocari school, or was it something -- are you talking of something completely different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to the extent that I'm aware, this piece of equipment had been removed from the elementary school earlier on. I was not aware of this device until as late as 1992. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. didn't know it was being used. In 1993, I had more information on this. I had more information on why it was used and how it was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it strange --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Richardson, if you want to pursue this matter, of course feel free to but I don't think it's that important.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So that we're clear, the RUP-12 that was in Pale was as far as you know operational in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Based on the information that I received later, it was operational. I told you about the purpose that it was used for, to listen to the Serb side, to use it to find out what was going on around Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Becirovic, that other RUPs were captured by the Muslim forces that you know of during 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what I know. At Zaluzje, another RUP-12 was found that had been damaged by the Serbs. They fired bullets at this piece of equipment. In the second half of 1992, some spare parts belonging to this bit of equipment were used in addition to those that had been found in the ruins at Potocari to try and piece together a proper radio device.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was that done?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said it was in the second half of 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as far -- I'll rephrase the question. Was this -- was -- you stated that there were a number of RUPs that were fixed, and I believe you mentioned -- or could you tell us what areas were in possession of these RUPs and what year?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of 1993, several bits of equipment had been mended, four or five or six of them if I remember correctly. There was one in the Potocari area, one in the Suceska area, two in the area of the town itself, and one was always kept as a spare option.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was the PTT building used to assist with repairing these radios, meaning your services or the services of other people in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Following demilitarisation, an electrical engineer Adem Bulbucovic - I think he's close to number 10 on the list that we looked at earlier - came to the PTT building and he fixed things as far as he could. He fixed the equipment. That's why it was necessary for all the bits of equipment that were out of order to be brought to one place so that the still-operational bits could be used to try and fix the other pieces of equipment. The premises of the PTT building were used for the simple reason that at the time, military observers of the UN and the UN police forces were stationed there. They allowed us to use 500 kilowatts of electric power. We used this electric power so that the technician could use the welder and any other bit of equipment that he needed. He needed power.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, were these radios -- was it necessary to recharge these radios? I think you may have alluded to that. Could you tell us whether all of the areas brought their radio to the PTT building to be recharged?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can we just fix the time period because we seem to be talking about after demilitarisation, and it's important for that be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what the witness said. If he's going to move from that period of time and include some other period of time, then he must tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second half of 1993, and just before the end of 1993 the need arose to try and use communications to create links between the various areas of the Srebrenica demilitarised zone. That's when the idea occurred to someone as of August 1993, I think, to collect all the radios that were not in good working order from the ruins, bring them to one place, and try to re-use them or re-use their spare parts that were still operational to maintain contact with areas that were outside the town itself. I can't remember the specific date when these devices were in fact mended and when they were distributed across the area, but I think it was back in December 1993, or maybe early 1994. I can't be sure about this. I know that we faced a great deal of trouble because we could not have direct communication from the Suceska area on account of the lie of the land. A mediator was needed to establish contact, and the device that was at Pale was used as a mediating piece of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was there an RUP kept in the Territorial Defence headquarters in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the end of 1993 there was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the radios were used for listening. Do you know if the radios were also used, the RUPs were also used by the Muslim forces to communicate with each other?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the second half of 1993 or just before I found out that there was a radio at Pale. I was told that this radio was mostly used for listening, or rather for listening only and that it was not being used for communication between members of the Territorial Defence. The simple reason was, there was no other equipment. In order to have proper radio communication, you must have two sides, two ends, so to speak at least, two participants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, do these RUs, do they work on AC, DC, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these could only be used on DC, 12 volts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, at the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we're approaching a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and -- okay. Let's have the break. How much more, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, another 20 minutes at most, if not 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue and finish, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, if you will, I would ask you to keep your answers short so that we can conclude the examination-in-chief. Just quickly with respect to the Iskra, as a general matter, is it possible for -- well, I'll rephrase the question. You mentioned that there was one in Srebrenica, one was in Konjevic Polje. Was there one in Potocari as well?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each local commune that was part of Srebrenica municipality before the war had at least one of these, so I believe there had to be one in Potocari as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during 1992 and 1993, as far as you know, was there one in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of, not from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to the Atlas, as a general matter, was it possible for communications to be conducted between Srebrenica and Cerska using this -- this radio?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to move to another area and ask if you recall the use of any other type of communication equipment being used by any member of the territorial -- of the TO, Territorial Defence, other than the ones we've already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any of the members of the TO using any other type of equipment other than the ones that we have referred to. Maybe your question was about whether it was possible. I remember that in September 1992, Naser Oric used a hand-made [as interpreted] radio, or rather he was carrying it around. It's a very small radio that you could put in your pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is that hand-made or hand-held?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The transcript, Your Honour, reflects hand-made. I just want to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. In this age, day and age, I wouldn't be surprised. It's a hand-held radio that you are referring, not hand-made? I mean, let's take it for granted that it is not hand-made. I mean, come on. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hand-made radios we used to make with crystals when I was 8 and 9 years old, and that time is a long passed now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only seeking to clarify to make sure it's not a mistake in the transcript or translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So could tell the Trial Chamber when it was that you observed -- I believe you've already said it, but could you tell us how many times you observed Naser Oric with this hand radio?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that I only saw Naser Oric very rarely. There were no details of note as far as I was concerned in relation to communications equipment, except perhaps, as I said, in September 1992 when I noticed that he was carrying this hand-held radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell if this radio was in use, operational? Was he using it at the time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. If he used it, I was never around; that much is certain. He didn't use it in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And other than September, did you see him with it at any other times during 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time when Naser Oric wished to talk to his family in Slovenia, he would come to the PTT building and he would make contact. This happened once a month or less, once every two months, depending on the situation that prevailed in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'd like you to concentrate on his use of the hand-held radio. Did this only happen in September or did you see him some other time using this radio or possessing it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness was crystal clear. He said he had never seen Mr. Oric use this equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, to a specific question that you asked earlier on, whether it was in working order, he gave you a very categoric answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Other than September of 1992, did you ever see Naser Oric in possession of this hand radio?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any details. I can't remember the details of every time we met. It's possible that he carried this radio around. It's possible he had it on him every time he came around. I simply don't remember any details. What I do know is he didn't use it in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you know the make of that radio? Because you seem to be quite familiar with the makes, types, of all kinds of radios. So perhaps getting a glimpse of it you would know immediately what radio it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I didn't recognise the make. Judging on what the situation was like following demilitarisation, it must have been 2G at the end, and it was a Japanese device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And other than Naser Oric, did you see any other members of the Territorial Defence in possession of one of these hand radios?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's be specific --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Hand-held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because one of these hand-held -- you need to be specific. Exactly the same or any kind of hand-held radio?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: As Your Honour just pointed out, either the one similar to the one that you observed Naser Oric with or any other type of hand-held radio?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also saw Ibrahim Mandzic carrying around a similar radio. But no one else except the two of them, not before the end of 1993. I did not notice anyone else carrying around these very small portable radios. That's why I referred to it as a hand radio because it's hand-held.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like have to a video shown to the witness. They are approximately three clips, and they're two minutes each, so we can go through it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, if you -- you just observed the video. Can you identify who's in the video. Do you see Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You asked him if he could identify, why don't you leave it at that, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was trying to avoid everyone else being identified in the interests of time. But I understand. I can just --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, I'll rephrase the question. In this video you're looking at at the moment, can you identify anyone in the video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, make sure -- have you received interpretation, Mr. Becirovic? Yes. So -- usher, could you please make sure that the witness has a picture, because from what I can see from the reflection, he doesn't have that, he has got something else. Yes. Do you recognise anyone in that still?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the person to the left of the civilian wearing a red jacket could be Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, to the left of the person wearing the red jacket. Yes. Do you see an arrow now pointing to a person on the screen? Is that the person -- is that the person you're telling us, according to you, is Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this could be Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. You don't need to tell us about the others for the time being. Yes, Ms. Richardson, next question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise. Just for the record, I'd like to indicate on the video the time is 39.13.4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that the arrow was pointing the -- to the second person from the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I think we may need to go back. I'm not sure the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, do what you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if he saw the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, the piece of equipment that you see Mr. Oric holding in this video, is that similar to the one you saw him with in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is similar. Actually, judging by the antenna that I can see in Naser's hand, I believe that this is a radio equipment, a piece of radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We can move to the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this person depicted in the video?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And for the record we are at 5 -- is it 5 or 6 that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's a --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe it's a 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 5 minutes, 55.5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We can continue the clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are the words important, relevant, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, they're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So why don't we -- let's come to the question because --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll move to the next clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you don't have any questions on that part of the video?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Becirovic, if you could look at the person that's depicted on your screen. Could you tell us if you could identify that person?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The device that he's holding in his hand, does that appear to be similar to what you observed him with in September of 1992? And perhaps we can let the video play for a moment before you respond.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any more questions with respect to this video. Just for the record, it is 23.29.27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, other than the radio communication that you've been testifying over the last two days, could you tell us if there were other means of communication in Srebrenica that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I was not aware of anything else existing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Other than the radios themselves, were messages relayed in any other manner?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like the witness to be shown Prosecution Exhibit 3, with the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, the document that is before you, I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 2, number 2. Just for the record, it is dated 18th October, 1992. And I would ask you to read that paragraph to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, are you aware of the use of couriers to relay messages -- or to communicate, I should say, in Srebrenica during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that couriers were used as such, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This is the first time you've -- you're hearing about the use of couriers, upon examination of this document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear that couriers were used. I am not aware of the existence of any such service in the territory of Srebrenica during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So during this period of time -- well, I -- let me rephrase the question. Were you aware that individuals were used to relay messages with respect to any matter?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, I just have a couple more questions for you and then I will complete my examination. You've testified that there were various means of communication by radios, whether it's the RUPs, Iskra, Atlas, et cetera. And I'd like you to take a look at the next document, Prosecution Exhibit 208.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm advised that we will also be handing out English translations as they weren't part of the exhibits previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say 208 or 28?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: 208, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 208. Okay, thank you. I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, please read that document that's before you. Now, with respect to this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: For the record it is ERN number 03721371, 03721371; it's actually one page. And I neglected to put the ERN for the last exhibit, Prosecution's Exhibit 3. Your Honour, if I can be permitted to do so now. For the record it is 0092-6461.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the author of this document, are you familiar with Ramiz Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has already told us about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can move through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just ask him whether this is his brother because he has explained this to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can go through it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is this person, Ramiz Becirovic, your brother?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did he work with the territorial staff and with Naser Oric during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, he did. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And is he a former JNA officer? Do you remember his rank?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he was a reserve officer of the JNA and he was a captain, a reserve captain. He never completed a military academy. After having served his compulsory service, he was recruited to become a member of the reserve. That's how things were done in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Right. Now, having read this document, does this confirm and reflect the communication -- that communication existed among the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think this witness can speak to that really. It's not a document either sent by him or received by him. If the Chamber is to draw any inferences about this document, then the Prosecution can invite you to do so at the appropriate time, but I don't see how this witness is going to give helpful evidence on that point. I also wanted to note that it was a bit of a liberty of my learned friend to insert Ramiz Becirovic there when, according to the English, it's illegible. That evidence has been given by the Prosecution, that it's Ramiz Becirovic; the witness hasn't said that. That's my first objection. That stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to the crux of the matter. This document says: "As agreed with Naser, do not prepare anything. Be on the alert if Naser needs you and wait for further orders." The important part to the Prosecution: "Put the radio station into operation in immediately and keep regular contact by means of communication. This order has been received through radio communication." Let's take the second part, the second sentence: "Put the radio station into operation immediately and keep regular contact by means of communication." Can you give us any information on what this could possibly mean? What were they referring? What was the author or signatory referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know, Your Honour. I'm really not clear on this, especially this second sentence where it says: "Put the radio station into operation immediately and keep regular contact." And this order was received by radio communication. I don't know whether the reference is made to the contents of this text or some other order. And if the reference is made to the contents of this text, I don't know why this was done. But what I know is that during this period of time there were no communications means, and I don't think that it was -- I don't think that it was possible to send any information by any communication means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was the brigade commander at the time, Karadzic, a person by the name of Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that at that time there were brigades. At that time there are just poorly organised groups of people, so I really don't make any sense of this address where it says that the letter should be sent to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The brigade commander, Karacici, would that mean the brigade commander at Karacici or the brigade commander named Karacici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a village in the territory of Srebrenica municipality, the name of which was Karacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was a radio station at the disposal of the brigade commander in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of the existence of radio stations at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The last sentence in this document says: "This order has been received through the radio communication." And it is then -- says: "By authorisation from the commander." Have you got an idea as to how the commander could have communicated with Ramiz Bec -- whoever it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your questions, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, were you in the field during the various actions taken by the Muslim forces during 1992 and in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Save for the period when I went to Cerska, I did not leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that was my final question. And I would like to put on the record, the video -- the video clips that were used, Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What exhibit is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prosecution's Exhibit 318 and Prosecution's Exhibit 434. I believe there's another one, if you could give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two, two. We saw two.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, just two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Madam Vidovic. So for the record you've been cross-examining [sic] this witness eight hours and 20 minutes, 22 minutes, Ms. Richardson. Three hours and 20 minutes more than you had told us you would be examining him. Anyway, we'll come to that later on. Which leads me to confirm to you, Ms. Vidovic, that you can take all the time you need to finish your cross-examination. But after your cross-examination, after this witness, then we are going to tell you, both sides, how long each witness is going to be in the box. And there will not be one single concession to either of you after this, because on this score if we allow things to happen in the same way they have been happening all along - we've been very liberal and open-handed - we won't finish before July, my anticipation. So Madam Vidovic -- what's going to happen now, Mr. Becirovic, because I am not quite sure that you are familiar with court proceedings. Ms. Richardson has finished with her examination-in-chief.
