She might have some further questions to you after Madam Vidovic has finished with her cross-examination. But now we are going to start with the cross-examination. Madam Vidovic is defending Mr. Oric, and she has every right to put all the questions that she needs to you. And you have the same responsibility in -- pursuant to the oath that you've taken to answer all the questions that are put to you truthfully and fully and precisely as much as possible. Okay. Yes, Madam Vidovic. If you want to sit down, you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This would certainly help.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Becirovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will put a number of questions to you and I would kindly ask you to reply by yes, no, or I don't know whenever you can. This will help us to save time. Obviously this is only on a condition that you are able to give such an answer.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Becirovic, you've told us that you were born and raised in the territory of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war you resided in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From December 1984, and before that I lived in my native village.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your native village is Opetci, which is in the local commune of Suceska. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war and during the war, your parents resided in the area of Suceska?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the months that preceded the war in February, March, and April 1992, you visited your parents in Opetci. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The local commune of Suceska borders on Vlasenica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, is that as early as autumn 1991 in the forests around Vlasenica and Milic, it was forbidden to fell timber because of the number of soldiers and ammunition that were deployed in the area. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that directly. However, from the beginning of 1992, the -- it was said that in the municipality of Vlasenica, all the felling had stopped, and this is the area bordering on the local commune of Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The persons from whom you heard that, did they tell you that this had something to do with the soldiers that were deployed there and the arms that had arrived in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned this from my parents, who had learned that something like that was happening, that all the felling had stopped. At that time, there were -- there was suspicion that there was military training taking place in the vicinity of Milici and that there was a lot of weapons to be had there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, that from the woods in the vicinity of Milici, between Milici and Suceska, one could hear constant shots that indicated that there was training going on in that area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My parents would tell me that shooting intensified at the beginning of 1992, maybe in February.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they make any sort of connection between the shooting that they heard and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a certain degree of fear because it was a well-known fact that in Milici there was an armoured unit of the former JNA that had probably arrived from Croatia and was deployed in Milici. I don't know exactly when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In March 1992, the Serbian Democratic Party made a decision on the division of the municipality of Vlasenica into the Muslim part and the Serbian part; that was a generally known fact. Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time the police forces from Milici and Tisca together with the brigade from Sekovici set up check-up points in the area. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As early as April -- I apologise, February 1992, the Serbs started setting up checkpoints in the places where they had majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They could stop people, check people, and they started mistreating Muslims, specifically, too, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago you referred to the armoured mechanised brigade, which you said had arrived from Croatia. It's true, isn't it, that this brigade was deployed in Sekovici and Lukic Polje?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about how this unit was deployed. It is a fact, to my knowledge at least, that part of it was in Milici and part of it in Lukic Polje. There was an armoured unit of the former JNA there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In February and March 1992, this was something that you could see everyday along the Sekovici-Milici-Rupova Brdo road, tanks and APCs moving along the road. Wasn't this the case?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All civilians who as early as May 1992 had fled to the local commune of Suceska who were saying that the manoeuvres of the Serb armoured units had been stepped up since about a month or two near the bauxite mine in Podravanje and this is the road that runs just next to the Suceska local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: People said that the soldiers you could see on tanks and APCs wore uniforms and also wore Chetnik insignia from World War II. Is this also something you heard?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you mentioned that before the war the reserve units of the JNA were trained in Milici. My question is about this: These reserve units were actually local Serbs from the area, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslim employees of the bauxite mine were saying that ever since the beginning of 1992 their Serb workmates had stopped coming to work and that they were being mobilised into the reserve units of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This training did not comprise Muslims, did it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Muslims carried on with their daily jobs at the bauxite mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the Serb population in that area, as early as April 1992, had already been mobilised and armed. Would I be right in claiming that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also heard that weapons had been given even to boys and to elderly men. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People, refugees for the most part, those who had been expelled from the Muslim villages after these villages had been burned, that when the Serbs first attacked and started torching villages they also saw children carrying firearms.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 21st of April, 1992, in Vlasenica, the Serbian authorities were established as well as a Serb police station. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the date, but it is a fact - and this applied to all the other municipalities that there were - that the Serbs established their own so-called Serb bodies of authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb police force led by Rade Bjelanovic and the Serb Territorial Defence, with the support of JNA units, set out to disarm the Muslim villages. Is this something you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now, please. I would like to show the witness a map. This is Prosecution Exhibit P520. Your Honours, we shall not be asking the witness to mark anything on the map, but we want him to show the Chamber around this map so that the Chamber can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is the same map that you used the other day to show the Muslim villages around Srebrenica when prompted to do so by the Prosecutor. I will now ask you to show some other villages. If you can please use the pointer and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Vidovic. Bear with me, please. Usher, I think we will need to put it on the ELMO. The only thing we require from you, Madam Vidovic, is more or less since the map is pretty big in size, let's divide it into four parts and you just indicate which part -- which quarter the usher needs to concentrate upon, whether it's top, right, left, left-right, or bottom left-right, left-right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the left part of the map, and the witness is familiar with the area, the area around Milici and Suceska. That is in the middle of the map and to the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, we have it. But -- usher, do you have problems? Because if you do have problems, bring it here and I will indicate to you which part you need to concentrate on. Yes, can you put the witness's --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you can give us a hand here. You're familiar with the Milici area, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, we have to move -- yeah, further to the left, Madam Usher, please. Yes. Just a little bit further to the left, please. You see Milici there where the two lines intersect. Yes, all right. Now, if you can -- if you can centre that and then we start zooming in. All right. You need to bring it down. Yes, perfect. We are almost there. Thank you. And then you can push it a little bit to the left and -- yes. Ms. Vidovic, go ahead, if we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe we can go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please now show Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nova Kasaba. Suceska.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be the Suceska area, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then Milici.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Milici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if you see Zaklopaca on the map, please show it. If not, please show where you would expect it to be. Do you agree with me that Zaklopaca is at the very entrance of Milici?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zaklopaca is more towards Vlasenica, the distance from Milici is seven or eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Can you please show Opetci, your own native village, on the map?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nurici?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nurici, Vlasenica municipality, if I can explain. You have the Srebrenica municipality facing Vlasenica here, and then you have the Jadar River canyon right here. And to my right you see Vlasenica municipality, and to my left you see Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation, Witness. Can you now please show Basta.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's near Nurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Pomol.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pomol is just above Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Stedra?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stedra.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Gornje and Donje Vresinje. Johovaca?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donje Vresinje, I can't see it on the map, but it's right next to the road. When you travel from Milici to Dobravanje [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Here and Dzile.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the witness is off the mike. We can't hear a thing he is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here and Dzile.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll ask you about some other villages, too, later. If you can't see them on the map, you can just put a mark where you think they should be. The Serb police and the Serb Territorial Defence carried out coordinated attacks against Muslim villages around Nova Kasaba and around Suceska in April, May, June, and July of 1992. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Kasaba started a little earlier, but Suceska happened on the 1st of May. There was an ultimatum for the Muslim population of Suceska to hand over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After Vlasenica was taken, the Serb police started to bring people in, beat them, and kill them, I mean the Muslims, in this area. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite right. It's a well-known fact that in the vicinity of Vlasenica there was a camp that was established, the Sucice [phoen] camp, where many of the -- of Vlasenica's Muslims were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about hundreds of Muslims that were killed in the camp, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of May, 1992, an atrocious crime -- a horrific crime was committed in the village of Zaklopaca, the village that you've shown us a while ago near Milici, when about 100 civilians were killed, including women and children. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The entire Muslim population of Zaklopaca was killed in a single day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, 1992, the following villages were torched: Piskavice and Dzandzici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The villages you've referred to are near Vlasenica, near Vlasenica town. I heard about this because I met people from the area. I met people who had fled the area in order to avoid being arrested. First they went to Cerska and eventually they arrived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As for the fate of the Muslims of Vlasenica, this is something that people in the Srebrenica area, especially in Suceska area, were quite familiar with, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In late May and early June 1992, the following villages were torched and destroyed: Durici, Sadici, Gradina, and the Muslim population of the village of Torina was killed. Am I right? Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the Muslim villages around Vlasenica were torched at this time. And those inhabitants who had not managed to escape were taken to the concentration camp at Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Opetci where you grew up and where your parents lived is in the immediate vicinity of the Muslim villages of Nurici, Basta, Tomo, Stedra, Gornje and Donje Vresinje, Johovaca, Here, and Dzile. Would I be right in stating that all these are in the vicinity of Opetci?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could see most of those villages with the naked eye. The Jadar River was the only natural line of division in the area. You could see from one hill to the next.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you referred to all these villages, saying that they had been torched. These were Muslim villages, which throughout June 1992 were torched by the Serb forces, weren't they, throughout May and June in fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These villages were torched in early May 1992. The torching started on the 2nd of May and continued several days later. Within less than a fortnight, all the villages had been torched.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Suceska could actually see the Serbs torch and loot these Muslim villages, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was one of those who could see, unfortunately. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, you said you stayed in the village of Opetci between the 18th of April, 1992 and the end of May that same year. Would it be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore you personally witnessed those Muslim villages burning, you personally witnessed the looting of property from those villages. Am I right when I say that the looting was done by the Serb population of the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People who were trying to escape had managed to identify their neighbours, their former neighbours, or their workmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, all this Muslim property, including livestock, would end up in nearby Serb villages and areas such as Podravanje, Ruda Brdo, Rupovo Brdo, Milici, Derventa. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Milici-Podravanje road passes near the village of Opetci, doesn't it? Can you please show this road on the map, the Milici-Podravanje-Derventa road, if you could use the pointer, please, and show the road on the map.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Milici. This is the road. Derventa, 10 kilometres from Milici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Podravanje?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the road to Podravanje.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were in your native village in the period of time that I've just defined. You were in a position to see that this road was being used on a daily basis by tanks, APCs, and other military vehicles of the Serb forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, what is the distance between Derventa and Suceska?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local commune of Suceska begins at one of the entry points to Derventa, and if you look at this bit here, that is already the local commune of Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the town of Derventa is in the immediate vicinity of Suceska, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I completed my four years of primary school in Derventa myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The town of Derventa right from the very beginning of the war and throughout 1992 and later was used as a stronghold for the Serb army, and a large number of armoured units and artillery were stationed there. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct. There was a well-known story that the local population of Derventa and the surrounding Serb villages volunteered to go to Croatia and to join the war there, or they went as reserve forces, depending.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the Serb population in the vicinity of Suceska greeted the war well-prepared, well-trained, and well-armed. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were anyone to say that those were local village guards that the Serb population had in the area, that would by no means square with the truth, would it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the very fact that Serbs used to walk around in uniforms at the time, they were marching around with their tanks and armoured vehicles -- as I say, this very fact indicates that those were by no means regular village guards. Those were well-armed and well-trained people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Srebrenica area alone -- the Srebrenica area itself was in total isolation as far as the media were concerned from the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not watch the Bosnian TV, but we could listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could only watch Serb TV stations, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. TV Belgrade and TV Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, it's true, isn't it, that while the Muslim villages were ablaze in April, May, and June, the Serb media reported that the Muslim forces had been torching Serb villages. Is that correct? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. On the 2nd of May, as the village of Pomol was burning, which is near Derventa, it's a Muslim village. Its population was entirely Muslim. At 5.00 in the afternoon, I watched the TV Novi Sad news. Soon after, I realised that Pomol was on fire. I heard the anchorman on the TV Novi Sad say that Muslim forces had torched the Serb village of Pomol. I was greatly surprised, to say the least, and couldn't make heads or tails of this, except to chalk this down to Serb propaganda. Maybe there was some people among the Serb population who had refused to take part in combat, and maybe this was their way of trying to get those people, to persuade those people as well, to join the torching and all the other misdeeds that were being committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And in May 1992 you were staying in the Suceska area and you actually talked to refugees who had been expelled from the Muslim villages, that we've referred to, Nurici, Pesici [phoen], Dzile, and so on and so forth. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the Serb units had reached the elevations in the area already in April 1992 and placed their artillery, tanks, and mortars there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Starting with Podravanje and then moving on to Milici, all the hilltops near the Serb villages had mortars positioned on them. And prior to the 1st of May, there would be nighttime firing for the most part on the villages of the Suceska local commune. Bursts of fire from small arms could also be heard very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see or hear at the time that on Basta, Brdo, and Podravanje, there were lots of Serb infantry forces stationed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The places that you have referred to did have Serb forces and artillery placed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was as early as April 1992 and onwards that artillery fire was being opened on the civilian buildings in Suceska and Srebrenica itself from the positions. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please show the Trial Chamber Rogac.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Rogac hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then Milica hill.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it on the map, but it should be around here, between Rogac and Milici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Koprivno?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Koprivno and Koprivno hill right next to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Suceska area was under siege by Serb military forces that had arrived from Milici on the one hand and from Rogaci, Milic hill, and Koprivno on the other facing Konjevic Polje. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Rogac, Milica hill, and Kopriva had heavy artillery and multiple rocket launchers deployed on them, and these shelled the civilian population of Suceska and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Rogac elevation is notorious in the area. The Serbs on Rogac shelled the town and the places around Srebrenica every day, randomly, not targeting anything particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is true, isn't it, that this area - and I am referring to Suceska in particular as well as Srebrenica - was constantly shelled from the airplanes that flew from Serbia and the airport near Bratunac in the area called Ade Stale, or Stale. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now let me ask you something else. Since you are a native of Suceska, you hail from that area, you knew the population of the surrounding villages, including the villages that belonged to the Vlasenica municipality but were bordering on the territory of Suceska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I attended at the primary school in Derventa, I got to know a number of people that belonged to my generation. They all went to school with me. All the children from these villages went to the primary school in Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are aware of the fact that refugees from Vlasenica in the territory of Suceska towards Zepa rallied around Becir Mekanic and the prewar commander of the Vlasenica police station, Fadil Turkovic. Did you ever hear of these people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While I was staying in Suceska towards the end of April 1992, the refugees that arrived from the burned areas were saying that in the vicinity of Besic hill or even higher up in the woods, people rallied around these two persons, that each of them rallied a group of people around them, as they expected that the war would end soon and that they would be able to go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, that these groups were armed? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was mostly the weapons that belonged to the reserve troops of the civilian police or hunting rifles that people had from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, that these groups were independent and they had nothing to do with Zulfo Tursunovic group in Suceska, but they shared the same area?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These groups also struggled to obtain food and arms, and they fought for those with the local Serbs from the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1992, or around that time, you were in Potocari when the shelling of Potocari and Srebrenica started?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Srebrenica was occupied on the 17th of April, 1992. Many people were killed there. Isn't that correct? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. The ultimatum was given on the 18th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: By the 9th of May, 1992, many people who stayed there, the elderly, women, and children, were killed. Over 80 houses were torched. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. In the town itself one street which had over 80 houses in it was completely torched. In those houses, the elderly people found their death.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The property of the Muslims of Srebrenica was looted, and this also includes the property of state institutions. The Serbs looted the Muslim property and the property of the state institutions of Srebrenica. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Whatever could be taken from Srebrenica was taken within a very short period of time. Everything was looted, whatever could be looted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the death of Goran Zekic, the Muslims returned to Srebrenica; you were among them. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have described the military situation in the territory which was held by the Serbs around Srebrenica. You will agree with me, won't you, that when it comes to the level of equipment for fighting, what the Muslims in the area had and what you saw them having was far below what the Serbs had?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the Muslims had very little weapons and uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were very small groups that had uniforms and weapons, am I right, and particularly uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to uniforms, very few people had uniforms. I can't give you an estimate, but I can only say that there were very few men wearing uniform at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Intellectuals had left Srebrenica or more educated people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were very few people who had any military education whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that in the course of 1992, the Muslim villages of that area had only those organised armed groups that defended their own respective villages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called them poorly organised or armed groups. The fact is that they were few and far between and that they did not comprise of many men.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to that, they were intercepted by the Serb villagers and the Serb forces and they were isolated from Srebrenica. They were cut off from Srebrenica. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There are entire Muslim villages which were cut off from Srebrenica throughout 1992. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to show the Trial Chamber the area that you are familiar with, Skenderovici, Poznanovici, Dedici, Podkorjen and Brezovice. This is the area in the vicinity of the village of Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brezovice, Skenderovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Poznanovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Poznanovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dedici? You will agree with me that Dedici and Podkorjen are in the vicinity of Poznanovici even they may not be on the map.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now could you please show the Trial Chamber the villages of Pribicevac and Spat?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Pribicevac and this is Spat.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what are Pribicevac and Spat. Am I right in saying that these are actually elevations?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are elevations. The two elevations that are famous for the fact that during these two locations, in the course of 1992 and 1993, from April 1992 up to demilitarisation and even after that, from Pribicevac, the shelling of the town Srebrenica and the Muslim villages continued from there and from the oppose side.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So Poznanovici, Dedici, Podkorjen, and Brezovice were cut off from Brezovice by Pribicevac and Spat that were very, very famous Serbian strongholds. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a very important correction in the transcript. I asked the witness Poznanovici, Dedici, Podkorjen, and Brezovice were cut off from Srebrenica by Pribicevac and Spat, and the witness said, "Yes, you're right." And it says here cut off from Brezovice.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, am I right in saying that these villages that I have just listed were cut off from Srebrenica by Pribicevac and Spat. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe this is a good moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, these Muslim villages that we have just mentioned, I've mentioned, Poznanovici, Dedici, Podkorjen, and Brezovice are villages which were in the closest vicinity of the area of the village of Ratkovici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, as you know, many people fled Glogova after the massacre in Glogova and they ended up in the area of Cizmici. That was in May of that year. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was a large group of people led by Ejub Golic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know, don't you, that large groups of refugees lived in the forests around Voljevica, Zaluzje, and Biljaca. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These people were armed, some of them were armed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of them were armed, but a smaller number of men were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The expelled Muslims from the Skelani region, including Tokoljaci, lived in the forests throughout the summer and autumn up until the winter of 1992. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the winter of 1992 and 1993, there were two camps in the vicinity of Tokoljaci. One was Tokoljaci and the other one was Sulice. Those were improvised huts in the forest where the civilians from the territories of Skelani and Osat lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These groups -- in these groups there were also men with weapons who fought the local Serbs in order to get some more food and some more weapons. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you mentioned four large armed groups of Muslims. You mentioned Naser Oric's group, Zulfo Tursunovic's group, Hakija Meholjic's group and Nedzad Bektic's group?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also Akif Ustic. I didn't mention Nenad Bjekic. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't. Generally speaking, you did have contacts with some of the men from these groups?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, these groups were also not organised, they did not communicate with each other or their communication throughout 1992 was rather restricted?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were poorly organised groups which did not communicate with each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, that in addition to these groups that you have mentioned, the four groups, that is there were also many other armed groups that fought against the local Serbs absolutely independently and had nothing whatsoever to do with these four groups throughout the year 1992 up to the demilitarisation. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were in Srebrenica in late June and early July 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Srebrenica during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You tried to gather information about what was going on in the territory of Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the month of July, I did. I made an effort to gather information about what was going on in the territory of the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will then remember that before this testimony, you gave your statement to the investigators of the OTP. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had not heard of the attack on Ratkovici until the moment you arrived in The Hague. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In conversations with people from various areas about the situation during the summer and autumn 1992, you obtained information that every single Muslim village was under a lot of pressure to bear from the far more powerful Serb force?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I heard that from the wounded who were brought to the hospital in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Every single Muslim village in the vicinity of Srebrenica and Bratunac struggled to survive. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. People defended their families, their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And they fought a far stronger enemy who were their neighbours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: People from these Muslim villages wanted to help each other in their joint struggle for survival. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It actually depended on the good will of these people in those groups, whether they would help other groups or not. Or better say, if their own villages were not under attack, there were cases of these people going to help some other places that did come under attack. There were very few weapons, and that is why people who did not carry weapons could not be used if they wanted to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm looking at the transcript, hearing the testimony. We're hearing about the Muslim villages without any specifications about which ones. So perhaps we could have some type of concrete information about which particular Muslim villages this witness is referring to. He's used the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, point taken, Ms. Richardson. Madam Vidovic, I think that needs clarification from you by means of a further question. Or now that the witness himself has heard the exchange from him directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the villages in the vicinity of Srebrenica and Bratunac. Isn't that so, Witness? Is that the way you understood me?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely the way I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in light of how many villages were discussed, I don't think it would do any harm at this point for the village -- for the witness, excuse me, to give us examples of some of the villages in the vicinity of Srebrenica and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Fair enough I think that's a fair -- a fair request and comment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yes, Witness, could you give us some instances in support of your previous testimony. Mention some of these villages to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The villages of Bljeceva, Cizmici, Potocari, the villages in the local commune of Suceska. These are the villages that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also I've asked you about the villages from the area of Ratkovici, such as Poznanovici, Dedici, Podkorjen. Did you have these villages in mind as well when you answered my question?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you question well, and that was whether people helped each other, I would be more familiar with the area of Potocari and Cizmici, as well as the area of Bljeceva, the area of Suceska. At that time I was not so familiar with the events that took place in the vicinity of Ratkovici, Skenderovici, and other Muslim villages in that area, such as Brezovice. At that moment, I was not familiar with the details of whether people in that area helped each other. However, soon after the demilitarisation, I had an occasion to talk to people as to what had been going on in these areas. They would also tell me that if they had an occasion to help each other, if one village came under the attack and the other didn't, then they helped each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. The struggle for survival in the Muslim villages that you have mentioned as being familiar with was a very hard struggle, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those villages were subjected to shellings by Serbs on a daily basis and people were killed every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thousands of refugees were killed in a bid to return to their villages under cover of the night in order to get food. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a well-known fact that the inhabitants of Glogova went from Bljeceva and Cizmici in an attempt to go back to Glogova and get food. Many were killed. Likewise, the inhabitants of Voljevica tried to go back to Voljevica during the night in order to bring back food for their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly, if we could have a time period as to these events that the witness is testifying to, and it's been some time since we've referred to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. These two incidents that you've just mentioned, the Glogova and Voljevica, when did they occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was several months, maybe one or two months after the occupation and after the population was expelled. The general idea was that the war would soon be over, and people believed that they would soon be able to go back to their homes. However, the war dragged on. And the food situation in these villages was very poor. Therefore, these people tried to obtain some food to feed their families by going back to their own native villages. These attempts became frequent in November 1992 and continued in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These people from certain Muslim villages that you have mentioned had to walk dozens of kilometres in order to reach a place where they could get food and thus survive. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. And very often they came across minefields where many of them were killed. The Serbs had noticed that people were undertaking forages to go and find food, and they would lay minefields along the routes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They also ambushed these groups and killed people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were killed in ambushes, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now move on to a different subject. Mr. Becirovic, in late May 1992 you got in touch with Akif Ustic. You inspected the communications centre of Srebrenica municipality and found some equipment there. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the information centre you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the information centre, that's the one I mean. Thank you for setting the record straight. You found the KTIC5 and the KTIC-751 there, the equipment that you found later. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was at the information centre that I found the IC-745 and later at the public security station I also found the IC-751.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have described the equipment you found. This was in late May or June 1992. What, if anything, was operational, the two radios, would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first one I used was IC-745, and later on I think it was in July I also started using IC-751.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No other pieces of equipment that you ever found in 1992 were in fact operational. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you would be quite right. There was no other single piece of equipment in Srebrenica that was operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Phone lines out of Srebrenica were only operational for as late as the first half of July 1992. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Following that, the IC-751 and the IC-745, that's after the phone lines to Tuzla were down, these two pieces of equipment were the only lines of communication to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you also said that you found some encryption equipment as well as a fax machine. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a teleprinter or a telex. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore you tried to have encrypted, protected, communication with Tuzla but there was no reply from Tuzla. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout August 1992, you received a set of rules on how to set up encrypted communication with other corps, how to use the encryption methods. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not receive any documents from Tuzla. For a while, I had communication with the Territorial Defence district staff in Tuzla, but I used documents from before the war that were at the information centre already, ones that I found there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's a document by the District Defence Secretariat in Tuzla dated the 23rd of August, 1993, and signed by the deputy secretary, Nusret Mesic. Witness, if you could please have a look. This is about organising the encryption of confidential information in the Tuzla district. The date on the document is the 23rd of August, 1993. I will quote a brief portion, the brief relevant portion of the document. It says in a telex dispatch sent in August 1992, the republican minister of defence repealed the system of encryption of written information in the territory of the Republic of BH. The decision was based on reasons that were easy to understand, given the fact that the aggressor, too, had special documents for encryption, hereinafter KZ, and the system as a whole was abandoned. It goes on to say: "The encryption system for confidential information used telegraphic wire -- telegraphic lines that were almost entirely useless." Witness -- so, Witness, this document appears to show that the republican defence minister decided to stop using the encryption system. I have this to ask you about it: It is true that encryption telexes and the entire encryption system in relation to written information could not be used for communication with Tuzla from August 1992 onwards. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair statement. Ever since the second half of July, that's when the phone lines were disrupted, the encryption system could no longer be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I understood you correctly, when you said that you had not used the encryption system even in the run up to August 1992. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair statement. We never used the encryption system at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, please, and for it to be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this will be Defence Exhibit D?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 261. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: IC-745 was returned to the radio club in order to help maintain the civilian phone lines that had been disrupted. And ever since it was returned, it was only used for that purpose, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: People in Srebrenica faced constant problems with the power supply, and that's why the IC-745 was placed in the PTT building on the first floor in a room that was referred to as the switchboard. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among other reasons there were no stable sources of electricity. However, initially this radio, IC-745, was used by people to keep in touch as well as to keep in touch with the other station and the IC-751.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, but I want to ask you about something else. Please explain to the Trial Chamber what the switchboard is and what it's used for.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's something you have in every post office. It's a separate room containing a large number of cables used to -- used for automatic telephones in the area that the post office is in charge of. There is an automatic switchboard at the post office that caters for these telephones. In order for two such telephones to be able to communicate, if we are talking about a wire link, there had to be a cable from the post office to one phone and from the phone back to the post office.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, anyone who walks into that room would immediately spot on one of these walls some sort of a board, some sort of a device, and this would be the switchboard, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a part of the switchboard, something called a -- the inspection table. And it was from this inspection table that you could check whether phone lines and telephones were in fact operational in order to save time for the operator, because otherwise they would have to make the rounds, go through the entire area and check every phone individually, and this way they were able to use this inspection table.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The IC-751 was in fact placed on a table that was right in front of the switchboard, or rather the switchboard was behind any person that operated the IC-751. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "switchboard," I mean two things, but this inspection table was behind the operator's back. And the way the cables were placed, that was in front of the operator.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Another question in relation to this. If someone who was not conversant with this sort of equipment or not sufficiently conversant at any rate walked into this room, all they would see is a large number of sockets. Right in front of the person sitting there they would see something behind the person's back three by two metres roughly speaking. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite visualise every single detail. The inspection table or the size of the inspection table was two by one and a half or three by one and a half, not more than that. And the cables, this bunch of cables looked fantastic to me at first sight. It looked like a fantastic thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this switchboard and the inspection table had nothing whatsoever to do with the IC-751 piece of equipment that was actually being used. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right. Those devices were entirely unrelated and could not enhance any operations performed by IC-751.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The radio device itself, the IC-751, was not a particularly powerful or sophisticated radio and it wasn't considered as such, even at the time. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure how much time I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have exactly 12 more minutes, but regulate yourself -- probably you have the entire day for tomorrow because I don't think you have another witness lined up for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're free -- I told you, we exceeded the Prosecution time by a good number of hours. So you have the entire day for yourself tomorrow. So if you prefer to stop now, we can stop now. I mean, it's up to you to choose, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I could ask another three or four questions. I have one document to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We can stay until 7.00 or stop any time it's convenient for you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can I have the usher's assistance now. I would like to show the witness a document. This is a document produced by the 2nd Corps in Tuzla, the date is the 2nd of March, 1993. The document was signed by commander Hazim Sabic, and the document was addressed to the supreme command staff communications section.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, if you could please have a look. I will quote the first two passages, the first two relevant passages in this document. It says: "With regard to your telegram number 02/30-10 of the 28th of February, 1993, we hereby inform you that we still have not activated the document using the SS-1 code with Srebrenica because the document numbers do not match. And following your opinion, we will not work on this anymore." "As far as the application of KZ in the CV in Eastern Bosnia is concerned, we only have shortwave communication using code tables with Cerska and Srebrenica." Mr. Becirovic, would I be right in saying that this document indicates that in 1992 you only had communication with Tuzla, that's the only communication you had was this KT communication?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, you did not use codes before the 22nd of March, 1993, rather you used open-line communication to talk to them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Even after the 20th of March, 1993, I never operated any piece of equipment that could be used to pass on written information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. It's true, isn't it, that this line of communication was used to pass on brief situation reports and appeals for help?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't exactly call them reports unless what you have in mind --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Situation reports.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless you mean reports as in a newspaper report or a public announcement. All the information that was passed on from Srebrenica only had to do with the difficult humanitarian situation, with the spreading infections, and with the difficult medical situation throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Becirovic, no orders were issued by Tuzla, no regular military or other reports were ever sent there. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I never for a moment said that the military authorities in Tuzla ever tried to get in touch with anyone in Srebrenica. This was a one-way affair. Srebrenica was passing on information to Sarajevo and in part to Tuzla. Such information, as I have explained, usually information of a public nature and information meant for the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document please be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document bearing ERN 01856771 and the Serbo-Croat version and its -- will -- is being tendered and is being marked as Defence Exhibit D262.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, in relation to Major Velid Sabic from Konjevic Polje, you said you had only sent to Tuzla a single document produced by him. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I explained about that yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that he personally handed this document over to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was not handed over to you by Hamed Alic, nor did you request or obtain from him approval to send this document on. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no other documents or reports by the Bratunac Territorial Defence or by the Bratunac Crisis Staff that you forwarded in 1992 and up until March 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this completes this round of questions, and I would like to call it a day at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Becirovic, we are going to stop here and we will continue and finish tomorrow. I thank you for bearing with us and see you tomorrow in the afternoon, 2.15, in this same courtroom. Thank you.
